job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Felix Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at seven, cycle to the office in Eindhoven and spend most of the day testing control software for electrical substations, the boxes that switch power on and off across the grid. I write my test scripts by hand and run them on a bench with real relays. Lunch is with Jan, who started the same week as me. What wears me out is the morning standup, where my manager Pieter asks again why I'm not using the AI assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a better autocomplete and not much more. At work I'd keep doing what I do. Pieter would say he told me so about nothing, and I'd shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm relaxed about it. My job is to prove a relay trips when it should, and a chatbot doesn't make that easier. What nags me is rent. Rooms in Eindhoven keep going up, even with a good salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. I'd keep my test routine, keep paying my union fee and keep my six months of savings where they are. Maybe in two or three years I'd look at a small flat with my parents' help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit bored, even, because nothing happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent nags you. What does that look like month to month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I pay 780 for a room in a three-person flat, plus about 90 for bills. After that I still save around 700 a month, so it's no emergency. It just feels unfair when a landlord puts the rent up 12 percent in one letter, like Lotte's did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the union you joined. What does it do for you in a calm world like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's mostly a legal helpline and a pay scale. My dad drove a bus for thirty years and the union got him his pension, so I joined in my first week without thinking. I'd rather pay 20 a month for a rule book than hope the company stays kind.

say: I'd say it's a **better autocomplete** and nothing more.
At work I'd carry on as usual and shrug at my manager's "I told you so".
think: My job proves relays trip correctly, so I feel **secure** and a little bored.
My real nag is **rent**, which keeps rising even on a good salary.
do: Keep writing and running my test scripts by hand on the **relay bench**.
Keep saving about **700 a month** and paying the union fee.
feel: I feel **calm**, with a touch of boredom.
S0.quote: Rooms in Eindhoven keep going up, even with a good salary.
fieldNote: He is secure at work, and the only pressure he names is **rent**.
Union membership is inherited from his bus-driver father, not a reaction to AI.
He is the only one in his team who ignores the AI assistant.

steps.text: Keep testing substation software by hand and paying the 20 a month union fee
Save 700 a month towards a flat deposit with my parents' help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software is moving tasks around, and the people who benefit should share in it. I'd bring it up at the union meeting. Pieter would say it's the moment to use the assistant, and I'd say show me the safety case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my test writing is exactly what a model does fast: reading a spec and producing checks. If Pieter's team gets a tool that writes the scripts, he'll ask why he needs four juniors. I'd be one of the four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep testing by hand for the safety-critical parts, because no regulator will sign off on a script nobody understands. I'd ask the union to negotiate rules on how the company uses AI on staff. And I'd start saving a bit harder, maybe 900 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I like my work, and I don't like not knowing if it'll still be mine in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be one of four juniors. What would you say to Pieter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the grid isn't a website, and a wrong test means a town without power on a cold night. He'd listen, because he's an honest man, but he also answers to a budget, and budgets don't care about my feelings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Still no AI tools yourself, even in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd have to try one, I admit. I'm not proud of it, but I'm slow with new software and I don't trust what I can't read line by line. I'd try it on my own time, on a non-critical script, before anyone forces it on me.

say: Software is moving work around, and the **gains should be shared** with staff.
I'd ask my union to press for rules on how the company uses AI.
think: Writing tests from a spec is what a model does fast, so a **junior seat** like mine is exposed.
Regulators won't sign off on scripts nobody understands, which gives **safety-critical** work some protection.
do: Keep hand-testing the **safety-critical** parts and raise AI rules at the union meeting.
Raise saving to about **900 a month** as a buffer.
feel: I feel **uneasy**: I like the work and can't see three years ahead.
S1.quote: The grid isn't a website, and a wrong test means a town without power on a cold night.
fieldNote: He expects junior seats to shrink first but trusts **safety rules** to protect part of the work.
He admits he might have to try an AI tool, which he hates saying out loud.
His trust in Pieter is real but limited by the company's budget.

steps.text: Raise the AI-rules question at the next union meeting
Try one AI tool on a harmless practice script in my own time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not a plan, it's a shock. I'd tell friends the government should have a public jobs and income scheme ready already. At work I'd say nothing loud, because everyone would be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job as a junior tester is gone or changed beyond recognition by then. The people deciding where AI goes will be a handful of owners, and they won't ask a graduate from Eindhoven. I'm angry at them more than at the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd put every spare euro into savings and stop any plan to buy a flat. I'd join every union action going and lobby my local politicians. And I'd probably have to use the AI tools, ugly as that feels, to stay useful to my team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I picture telling my mum and dad that the degree they were proud of is worth less than a bus ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're angry at the owners. What would you actually do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to a demonstration, sign every petition and vote for anyone who talks about taxing the profits. It won't feel like enough, but sitting at home would feel worse. My dad always said you stand with your colleagues or you stand alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm fine for six months, I have savings, and I'm not asking for money yet. But I'd ask if I could move back to their place in Tilburg if rent became the problem. Saying that out loud would be hard.

say: Two years is a **shock**, not a plan, and the state needs an income scheme ready.
I'd keep quiet at work because everyone would be scared.
think: My junior tester job is probably **gone or unrecognisable** by then.
I blame the **owners** deciding where AI goes more than the software.
do: Pour spare money into **savings** and drop the idea of buying a flat.
Join every union action and write to local politicians about **profit taxes**.
feel: I feel **scared** and ashamed that my degree might be worth little.
S2.quote: My dad always said you stand with your colleagues or you stand alone.
fieldNote: Strong savings keep him at **anxious** rather than alarmed.
His anger goes at AI owners and politics, not at his manager.
Falling back on his parents in Tilburg is a plan he finds hard to say.

steps.text: Stop looking at flats and put 1,000 a month into savings
Join union actions and write to my local MP about taxing AI profits
Ask my parents if I could move back to Tilburg if needed
Vote for parties that promise an income scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for the unions and the government to act, if they start now. I'd push my union to put AI on the table in the next pay round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have a couple of years in the job and then a squeeze. By 2031 my seat is probably automated, but a team that checks the machines would still exist. I'd want to be on that team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the five years to move from writing tests to reviewing them, the person who signs off. I'd learn the grid standards properly and take a masters course in the evenings. I'd keep saving, aiming at a year of money in the bank by the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but not panicked. There's a road, and I can see where it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a year of savings actually give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to say no. If a firm tells me to hand my job to a model, I can take a term at university and not panic about rent. It's a cushion for a union fight too, if there's a strike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the grid standards. Why those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they're written by people and enforced by law, and I think law is slower than software. Whoever understands the standard can say if the machine got it right. That feels safer than being the fastest typist in the room.

say: Five years is enough if unions and government **start now**.
I'd push my union to put AI on the table in the next pay round.
think: By 2031 my seat is probably automated, but a team that **checks the machines** will still exist.
I'd rather sign off other people's work than race a model at typing.
do: Learn the **grid standards** and start an evening master's course.
Build a **year of savings** by the end.
feel: I feel **anxious** but can see a road ahead.
S3.quote: I think law is slower than software. Whoever understands the standard can say if the machine got it right.
fieldNote: The longer warning turns his fear into a **plan**: move from writing to reviewing.
He still avoids AI tools in this scenario, trusting standards over speed.
A year of savings is what lets him say no to his firm.

steps.text: Study the grid safety standards and aim to become the reviewer
Enrol in an evening master's course in power systems
Build savings up to a full year of rent and bills
Press my union to include AI in the next pay round

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels almost normal. I'd say people should start learning now and not wait to be told. At work I'd say let's see the actual tools first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not very worried. By 2036 I'd be 32, probably a senior engineer with a family, and whatever replaces my current job I'd have grown into something else. I'd still worry about the people in my dad's generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep the union fee going and buy a small flat in about four years. I'd try some AI tools casually, because by then even I would have to. And I'd put money into a pension early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A decade lets me imagine a life, with a flat and maybe a dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your dad's generation. What worries you there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad will be 66 then, and his bus route may be driven by software. His pension should be safe because of the union, but I'd still want it written into law, not just a promise. I'd feel bad if I had a good job and he had to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And would you still avoid AI tools until someone forces you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably I'd get to them in the end. It would be like email, I wouldn't choose it, but one day everyone's using it and I'm the odd one out. I'd prefer to learn on my terms, with the union asking what the tools do with our data.

say: Ten years feels almost normal, but people should **start learning** now.
At work I'd say let's see the real tools first.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32 and a **senior engineer**, grown into something else.
I'd worry more about my **dad's generation** than about me.
do: Buy a small **flat** in about four years and start a pension early.
Try AI tools casually, like I once started using **email**.
feel: I feel **mostly okay**, with room to imagine a flat and a dog.
S4.quote: A decade lets me imagine a life, with a flat and maybe a dog.
fieldNote: Time lets him picture a normal life, but he keeps a **family worry** about his father's pension.
He sees AI tools as something he'll adopt late, like email.
His mood stays uneasy because the end point still rests on owners' decisions.

steps.text: Buy a small flat in about four years
Open an early pension plan alongside my work one
Try AI coding tools once a month and ask the union about data rules

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because two years leaves no time for anyone to organise. What would help is a public jobs and income scheme already written into law, a union at the table when firms bring in AI, and clear rules on what an AI can sign off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I don't feel like a typical young tech person. I don't use these tools, I joined a union and I'd like the state to do more. People think my generation all wants to move fast, and I want to move carefully.

headlineQuote: I'd rather pay 20 a month for a rule book than hope the company stays kind.
portrait: Felix is a **22-year-old** electrical engineering graduate, testing substation software in Eindhoven and sharing a flat.
He is top of his class, saves **700 a month** and has parents who would take him back.
He is progressive and union-minded, and blames **AI owners**, not the software.
He avoids AI tools and moves slowly, so he is calm in a plateau and **anxious** when the clock is short.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries him most, because two years leaves no time to organise.
whatWouldHelp: A **public income scheme** in law, a union at the table and clear rules on AI sign-offs.
